text:
Nigeria has two separate $500 million loans involving the World Bank recently, but the similarity in their amounts has raised questions about what the funds are meant to achieve and whether they are part of the same borrowing arrangement.
The two projects are the Agro-Climatic Resilience in Semi-Arid Landscapes (ACReSAL) Project and the Nigeria Infrastructure Financing and De-Risking Platform for Growth and Jobs (INFRAGROW) Project.
Although both involve $500 million, one (INFRAGROW) is a loan request while the other (ACReSAL) has been approved by the World Bank. They have different objectives, implementing institutions, beneficiaries and timelines.
While ACReSAL is designed to tackle environmental degradation and strengthen climate resilience, particularly in northern Nigeria, INFRAGROW seeks to attract private investment into infrastructure development by providing financing facilities, investment capital and guarantees to reduce risks for investors.
There is also a difference in their approval status. The World Bank approved the additional $500 million for ACReSAL on November 6, 2026, while INFRAGROW remains at the project preparation stage, with approval estimated for May 25, 2027.
The $500 million ACReSAL financing is additional funding for an existing World Bank-supported project aimed at tackling environmental degradation and strengthening climate resilience in Nigeria.
The World Bank announced the approval of the additional financing on November 6, 2026, to enable Nigeria to expand interventions in vulnerable communities across the northern part of the country.
The project focuses on restoring degraded landscapes, rehabilitating watersheds, improving water management, controlling erosion and flooding, and strengthening the livelihoods of communities affected by climate change.
By 2031, the additional financing is expected to support the restoration of 1.4 million hectares of land and benefit approximately 6.6 million people.
The expected outcomes include improved household incomes, better soil health, increased agricultural productivity, reduced flooding and fewer conflicts among farmers, herders and communities.
ACReSAL is not a new project. It has been running since 2022. The World Bank reported that it has introduced sustainable landscape management practices on approximately 550,000 hectares and reached more than 4.4 million beneficiaries.
The additional $500 million is intended to expand the project’s existing interventions rather than establish an entirely new programme.
The Federal Ministry of Environment implements the project in collaboration with the Federal Ministry of Water Resources and Sanitation and the Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security.
It covers the 19 northern states and the Federal Capital Territory.
Unlike ACReSAL, the proposed $500 million INFRAGROW financing is designed to address Nigeria’s infrastructure funding gap by attracting more private-sector investment into infrastructure development.
According to the World Bank’s Initial Project Information Document, prepared on November 4, 2026, Nigeria requires approximately $100 billion annually to close its infrastructure financing gap.
The challenge is not just a shortage of money. The World Bank identifies inadequate preparation of bankable projects and the risks associated with infrastructure investments as major obstacles preventing investors from committing funds.
INFRAGROW is designed to address these problems by creating an integrated financing platform anchored by the Nigeria Sovereign Investment Authority (NSIA).
The proposed platform will use four specialised financial facilities to prepare infrastructure projects, provide financial support, inject investment capital and offer guarantees to reduce risks for investors.
Project Preparation Facility (PPF): This will provide funding for feasibility studies, project design, transaction structuring and procurement support to help turn infrastructure proposals into commercially viable projects capable of attracting investors.
Viability Gap Fund (VGF): This will provide financial support to economically important infrastructure projects that cannot generate enough revenue to attract private investors or sustain affordable charges for users.
Risk Capital Facility (RCF): This will provide equity and other forms of risk-bearing capital to commercially viable infrastructure projects that struggle to attract sufficient initial investment.
Credit Guarantee Vehicle (CGV): This will provide guarantees to protect lenders and investors against specified financial and political risks, making infrastructure projects more attractive to long-term investors.
Through these facilities, the World Bank expects INFRAGROW to mobilise additional domestic and international private capital for infrastructure development.
The project will also support reforms and strengthen the capacity of government institutions to identify, prepare, assess, procure and supervise public-private partnership projects.
The proposed project will be implemented by the Nigeria Sovereign Investment Authority, while the Federal Ministry of Finance will represent the Federal Government as the borrower.
Although the World Bank document identifies $500 million in proposed IBRD/IDA financing for INFRAGROW, the project’s total financing structure is estimated at $3.85 billion.
The proposed financing comprises $500 million in World Bank financing, made up of $400 million from the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD) and $100 million from the International Development Association (IDA).
It also includes $400 million in equity contributions, comprising $200 million from government resources and an indicative $200 million from private-sector investors.
Another $600 million is expected from commercial debt, while $2.35 billion is structured as guarantees.
The guarantees comprise a $100 million IDA guarantee and $2.25 billion in guarantees from other international financial institutions.
The World Bank document also indicates that the NSIA is expected to provide an indicative $200 million equity commitment as the platform’s founding shareholder.
This means the $500 million is the proposed World Bank loan financing component, not the entire amount expected to be deployed through the platform.
The larger financing structure is designed to leverage additional public and private investment and provide guarantees that reduce investment risks.
The $3.85 billion is therefore the proposed total financing structure, not a $3.85 billion World Bank loan to Nigeria.
